Tomato Receipts.

German Postal Worker Sentenced
to Year for Shortage.
BERLIN (/Pi.-German judicial
severity, traditionally , characteristic of
pre-war days, has not entirely subsided
under the republic. This was showr.
t hen Gustav Schroeter, for 26 years
a servant of the government, first in
the army and since 1920 in the postal
service, was sentenced to a year in
prison for a discrepancy of $1.30 in
| his books.

The prosecution alleged that
Schroeter had manipulated his accounts bo
that a deficit of $3.80 which he had to
refund was reduced to $2.50. The
defendant insisted that the discrepancy
was due to errors in bookkeeping.
His wife was present in court and
collapsed In a dead faint when Justice
Boetge pronounced sentence "for the
good of the postal service."

i
; IN STOCK DELIVERIES
.' Shortage of Blanks May Keep
| Buyers Waiting for Next
Six Weeks.
Howard B. Smith, chairman o.' the
, New York Stock Transfer Association,
■ predicts some long delays in the
delivery of stock certificates. The reason,
i of course, is the appalling number of
transfers to be made following last
week s panicky trading, making it simply
impossible to enforce the 48-hour rule.
Most stocks are deliverey in 100-share
lots. Then if there are hundreds of
small orders these certificates have to
be split to mee the odd-lot requirements.

This requires the making out of new
certificates with the names of the new
owners, an almost endless amount of
work being involved under present
conditions.
Big corporations always keep a large
quantity of blank stock certificates on
hand. In many instances this supply
has been exhausted. This unusual
condition means a delay for printing. So
serious is the situation that one local
investment banker said today that he
believed some of the stock bought last
week could not be delivered for six
weeks.

Turkish Women
Win First Strike
For Higher Wage
By the Associated Press.
KASTAMUNI, Angora.
November 4. - For the first time In
history Turkish woman workers
have gone on strike. They won.
The strike was inaugurated by
2.000 Anatolian peasant women,
still wearing their veils. They
were employed by the Turkish
Forest Exploration Co. They
walked out because they received
only 25 cents a day, half of the
wages paid men.
They demanded wages equal to
the men's and their employers
promised to cease economic dis- ''
tinction between the sexes in the
future.

SLAYING SUSPECTS
ARE REFUSED BOND
Two Held for Murder of Borger
Prosecutor Deny
Guilt.
By the Associated Presa.
BORGER, Tex., November 4. - After
a brief respite from notoriety, Borger,
boom town of the Western prairie oil
fields, was again in the limelight today
as two men were held without bond for
the murder which led to the town's
recent occupation and rule by Texas
National Guardsmen.
Sam Jones, deposed deputy
constable, and Jim Hodges, manager of a
boiler works, are charged with the
murder of District Attorney John A.

Holmes last September 13.
Officers went to New Mexico for
Jones, arresting him on a liquor law
violation indictment. Hodges was
arrested at his home here. Both men
deny any part in the crime.
Last night District Attorney Clem
Calhoun conferred with Hedges. What,
he learned was not divulged. That
the prosecutor believes he is on the
right track was attested by his
statement that before the new year John
Holmes' murderer will be punished.
At Stinnett, county seat of
Hutchinson County, another echo of Borger's
turbulent period was heard in the
murder trial of William J. "Whitey"
Walker, docketed for today. Calhoun
said he would ask for a continuance in
Walker's case, to allow him time for
further investigations.

Walker's trial was called the most
important pending when Holmes was
murdered. He was in jail at Stinnett
at the time.

FOR FLORIDA FRUIT
Sweden Removes Duty on
Oranges - Other Countries
Increase Orders.
Special Dispatch to The Star.
WINTER HAVEN. Fla.. November 4.
Florida fruit is gaining such popularity
in certain European countries as to
merit serious governmental and
commercial attention. Sweden, for
example, this year enacted legislation
removing the duty of 70 cents a box on
Florida oranges. According to a report
of the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic
Commerce, the step was taken upon
the advice of the Swedish medical
au! thorities, who are encouraging greater
consumption of citrus fruits.

The Florida Citrus Growers'
Clearing House Association has just been
advised that the South Atlantic
Steamship Line has materially increased its
citrus fruit refrigeration
accommodations for the exportation of oranges and
grapefruit to Liverpool. Demand for
grapefruit has been steadily increasing
in England for several years. The cost
is much higher than in this country
i and the smaller sizes are mostly in
demand. In that country, too, prominent
| physicians are urging the people to eat
| more citrus fruits.
j In some of the exclusive resorts of
1 Northern Europe last year Florida
j grapefruit found a ready market at
prices ranging from SSO to 100 a
j box, which means that the table charge
' for half a grapefruit was often well in
excess of the equivalent of an
American dollar.

To date the bulk of the 1.000,000
boxes of grapefruit and oranges which
have been shipped out of Florida since
last month has been sold in the
mar: kets of New York, Philadelphia, Boston
i and Chicago.

ANY individuals have been held responsible for the stock
market crash. Some have mentioned Jesse Livermore,
and a few have spoken with bitterness of President Hoover's
fairly recent market letter.
My friend Morris Ernst, the lawyer, introduces a new
culprit. He is inclined to blame it all on Charles E. Hughes.
To be sure, Mr. Hughes stands to some extent as a symbol.
'His activities in New York state did much to make race
track gambling difficult, and if Gov, Hughes did not succeed
in ending the improvement of the thorobred at least he
drove it under cover.

Economists agree that at least the panic phases of the
great decline may be attributed to the evil consequences of
gambling. And in the situation there will be an attempt to
discourage the public from ever again indulging in a
passion for games of chance. Yet it is quite possible to argue
that, instead of having less gambling, we should have more.
Perhaps our present difficulties arise from the fact that we
have been too cavalier in checking what is, after all, a
deepiv rooted human instinct.

TN England, for instance, the white collar class goes in
- yery heavily for race track betting. But in this same
group the stock market plunge is far less common. Here it
is rather difficult to get a bet down on a horse, and so the
man with a small sum to risk has been tompted to trust it
to something gilt-edged, like United Corporation or
Standard Brands.
In the long run which community is better off? It seems
to me best to recognize the gambling instinct and legalize
it. To be sure, the small bettor at the English track quite
often sacrifices his all, but I doubt that any meeting has
ever spread losses so widely thru the community as our
recent Wall Street crash.

After all, there are certain advantages which work for
the man who bets on horses rather than stocks. When the
bookmaking is on an open cash basis the patron can lose
only what he puts up. It is never the custom for a
commissioner to rush to him, while the horses are in the
stretch with the request that he sweeten his wager on
l'appyrus or be sold out. Nor is it ever necessary to dig down
for additional funds to support the favorite just as he
approaches the water jump.

One day's transaction is complete in itself. You win or
you lose, but there is no need to be awake all night
wondering what your horse will open at in the morning.
IN the long run - and generally in the short run, as well -
every man who plays the races will lose money. Hut 1
think this is equally true of the small stocx market gambler.
And, after all, a good horse is a more gallant and beautiful
creature than American ami Foreign Power. A young man
of limited means is better off economically if he lets both
horses and Wall Street speculation alone. But this is the
counsel of perfection. There will always be young men
willing and eager to take a chance. Nothing that you or I
can say is likely to deter them. And surely it is rather

more fun to lose your savings under the blue sky while
thousands cheer them see them dwindle in b stuffy brokerage
office where there is only gloom.
Oil AW once said thru the mouthpiece of a character in one
• of his plays (1 quote from memory), "If you've got a
vice you can't get rid of make a virtue of it." I doubt most
dreadfully that the gambling instinct can be eradicated in
our lifetime by any sort of legislation. Accordingly, I think
it would be wise for the government to turn this passion to
its own advantage and to the advantage of the community.

Specifically, I suggest that the income tax be abolished and
that all necessary funds for Federal expenses be raised by
government lottery.
This would be the easiest of all taxes to collect. The
money woud roll in profusely, and nobody would be under

January night in 1928 that the
apartment house standing in the
Landsberger Allee, together with an
its contents, human and otherwise,
was flung skyward as the result of
the ignition of a pool of gas that a
leaky main had poured into the
cellar of the building.
Rescue workers, poking among
the piles of brick, twisted iron and
shivered furniture, managed to save
a score or more persons who had
been injured in the explosions, but
they also found the remains of 17
of the occupants who were beyond
all hope of rescue.

Berlin soon forgot the catastrophe
and, as tho wishing to help the
procoss along, the owner decided to clear
away the ruins and build anew.
Considerable insurance money was due
him and when this was forthcoming
he would begin.
Unfortunately the insurance
company had a somewhat different view
of the matter. Its inspectors were
of the opinion that the wreckage
need not be removed, that the
"building" could be repaired, thus
entailing a much smaller insurance
payment.
The matter was taken into one
court and then in another, without a
successful or acceptable solution
being reached. The case remains, in
a stalemate, while the ruins gather
moss and all the various debris of a
thickly settled neighborhood.

HAPPILY there are ways of get-,
ting around rules, even at the
price of a good rooster, as happened
in this particular instance. Some
miles down the line from a town
where a literal-minded station
master was employed there had been a
train wreck. Some twenty
passengers were in need of immediate
medical attention. ,
A hurry call was sent to the
railway physician in the nearby town.
He, in turn, rushed to the station,
and there, luckily as he thought,
found an express train ready to
depart in the direction of the wreck;
but when he sought to climb aboard
the station master curtly informed
him that the train did not carry
passengers.

No amount of argument could
induce the agent to change his stand.
He was sorry but his instructions
were plain and not
misunderstandable. He even went so far as to dig
up his rule book and show the
physician the regulation in question.
In part, it read, "passengers may be
carried only when necessary to
accompany livestock.
This gave the doctor an idea. He
ran to the nearest house, the
occupant of which, he knew, kept
chickens. He hastened back to the
station, chicken under his arm, and
after certain necessary billing
formalities was permitted to board j
the train.

INJURIES TO ENVOY
FROM ERIN SERIOUS
By Universal Service
Michael Mac White, minister of the
Irish Free State, who was struck by
a hit-and-run driver Thursday night,
was found yesterday to have five
broken ribs.
His condition is still serious.
Eleven stitches were taken in a
deep gash in his forehead, and It
was not until X-ray photographs
had been taken and developed that
surgeons at Emergency Hospital
were satisfied that the skull had not
been fractured.
President Hoover was among the
first to inquire as to the condition
of the diplomat when Minister of
Education Desmond Fitzgerald called
at the White House yesterday.
Minister Mac White was to have
introduced Fitzgerald to the President,
but William J. B. Macauley,
secretary of the legation, officiated in
his stead.

Both Fitzgerald and Macauley
were with Minister Mac White when
he was run down at Dupont Circle
last night. He was carried 15 feet
on the fender of the car and was
bleeding profusely when taken to
the hospital.
Mrs. Mac White was summoned to
Washington yesterday from New
York, where she was visiting.

Walter F. Brown, of Toledo, who is
rumored as President Hoover's
choice: Col. Carmi A. Thompson, of
Cleveland, who stepped out of the
senatorial race in 1928 in favor of
Senator Burton; Roscoe C.
McCulloch, of Canton, chairman of the
State Utilities Commission: E. W.
Edwards, of Cincinnati, banker and
friend of the governor, and William
H. Boyd, Cleveland attorney.

Hottest Here
In 14 Years
OFFICIAL thermometers
registered 76 here
yesterday afternoon - the highest
temperature for November 1 since
1915, when the mercury went
to 77.
At the White House, even
with doors and windows thrown
open, it became so warm that
President Hoover decided to
make another trip to his
summer camp in the Blue Ridge
-Mountains this week-end.
In the .Senate chamber, where
the refrigerating plant had
been turned off for the season,
those participating in the tariff
debate mopped their faces with
handkerchiefs.

Weather Bureau officials said
the fall heat wave was by no
means unprecedented. Records
show two occasions when
thermometers registered as high as
80 here in November.

Dr. William H. Perry
Dead at Cleveland, Ohio
CLEVELAND, Nov. 1 (1.N.5.). -
Dr. William H. Perry, 61, prominent
Cleveland physician, was found dead
In his room in a downtown hotel
here today. Death was caused by
heart disease.
According to friends, the physician
was accustomed to engage a room
at the hotel whenever he had an
early moyning operation. When he
failed to" respond to a call today,
hotel employes entered his room and
found dead.

Canvas Found
In Vienna May
Be a Da Vinci
Experts Now Engaged in
Making a Minute Ex*
amination
By WILLIAM HILLMAN
BERLIN, Nov. 1 (U.S.). - A
mysterious painting, believed to
he a long-lost canvas of Leonardo
Da Vinci, has come to light in
the Dorotheum, Austrian state
pawnshop in Vienna.
The painting, that of a woman,
Is worth between $1,000,000 and
$2,000,000 if it proves to be an
authentic work of the immortal
Italian, but officials of the
government pawnshop are keeping the
details of their discovery secret.

PAINTER SOLD IT
It is said that the painting was
discovered when a well-known
Viennese art dealer, believing the
portrait to be the work of some
unknown Florentine painter,
disposed of the canvas for 25,000
schillings, about $4,000, later to
find himself "sold."
The tine technical qualities of
the painting attracted the experts
of the Dorotheum, who began a
rigid examination. Although their
investigation is not yet complete,
they believe the canvas is a true
Da Vinci. The painting is that
of a woman said to be Ginervam,
wife of Amerigo Benci, painted in
1503, according to two of the
Dorotheum experts.

RIVALS MONA LISA
Others believe it was painted
around 1514, the period in which
Da Vinci produced the celebrated
Mona Lisa, and that this portrait,
which is being carefully hidden
from the public, rivals in quality
the famous Mona Lisa. Other
critics who have seen the canvas
are inclined to believe the
painting is the work of a Da Vinci
pupil.

CARNEGIE FUND
AWARDS 51 FOR
HEROIGffIS
PITTSBURGH, Nov, 1 (U.P.). -
Two silver and 49 bronze medals
were awarded today for
outstanding: acts of heroism by the
Carnegie Hero Fund Commission.
Nineteen of the heroes lost their
lives in performing the acts which
the Carnegie Fund recognized.
Pensions aggregating 17.080 a year
were granted to dependents of
eight of these. To dependents of
eight others who lost their lives,
the sum of >4.800 was granted to
be applied at the commission's
discretion.
In addition to these money
grants, >14,400 was appropriated
for educational purposes in nipe
cases. Awards aggregating >17.500
were made for other worthy
purposes in 20 other cases. x
WOMAN AIDS RESCUE
Both silver medals were awarded
to persons who aided in saving
others from drowning. One of these
awards W'as to a woman and the
other to a man, who died in his

effort to save a life.
Miss Barbara H. Muller, 22;
Charleston, S. C., a student,
received a silver medal for helping
to save Mrs. Lucy W. Holley. 24,
from drowning at Sullivans Island,
S. C., on July 13, 1928.
Mrs. Holley was bathing in the
ocean and was carried 600 feet
from shore by an undercurrent.
After several men had attempted
to rescue the woman. Miss Muller
swam out to where Mrs. Holley
was struggling. She swam 20 feet
toward shore, carrying Mrs. Holley,
until a young man met her and
aided her in carrying the woman
to shore.

WIDOW BENEFITED
The widow of Howard R. Grundy,
of Miami, Fla., will receive a silver
medal and death benefits at the
rate of >75 a month, with an
additional $5 for her son.
Grundy, who was 44 and a
salesman, died while attempting to save
Mrs. Jodie T. Thatcher, 28, from
drowning at Miami Beach on
August 2, 1928. Grundy, after a long
swim, struggled for 20 minutes
trying to bring Mrs. Thatcher to
shore. He was drowned in the
attempt, but Mrs. Thatcher was
brought to shore and revived.

BUSINESS UNHURT.
DR. KLEIN DECLARES
Market Crash Not Expected
to Affect Firm Structure
of U. S. Industry.
By the Associated Press.
Official Washington citing steadfastly
today to its opinion that American
business need expect no adverse result
from the collapse of stock exchange
prices.
Su"h a view was expressed by Dr.
Julius Klein. Assistant Secretary of
Commerce, in a widely broadcast
address last night, over the National
Broadcasting System, which is
understood to represent the attitude of the
administration in general, and
coincides with President Hoover's previous
statement on the business situation.

No action had been takm by the
Federal Reserve Board, in the face of
yesterday's precipitous decline in
security prices, although the board met with
Secretary Mellon attending, and was
known to have been in close touch with
the Reserve Bank at New York.
Tydings Raps G. O. P.
The break in stock prices was
attributed to the party in power by
Senator Tvdings, Democrat, Maryland, in a
statement issued through Democratic
national headquarters. It asserted that
"in most cases there is the ironical
realization that these great leaders, who
a year ago were yelling 'prosperity' are
trying to find a scapegoat in the face
of a §15,000.000,000 loss In one week of
American life." ,
Dr. Klein cited numerous
circumstances to support his view that
American business is standing sQuarely upon
a firm, sound basis.

"The purchasing power of the
Nation is at a high level, he said, and
may be expected to continue so, the
demand for commodities has not been
affected by the stock market collapse;
employment is on the per
capita production booming, "
manufactured goods have not piled
and average commodity prices nave
maintained consistent levels.
"Regardless of regrettable speculative
uncertainties." he asserted, ''the
industrial and commercial structure of the
Nation is sound."
Hoover Statement Stands.
Pointing to President Hoover's
statement of last Friday on the business
situation which expressed high confidence
In the industrial structure of the
country. Dr. Klein said that no
interveriing* circumstance could be regarded as
necessitating a change in a single word
that the Chief Executive uttered.

At the most liberal estimate, he
asserted, only a very small proportion ot
the American population has been
affected bv the stock market
collapseless than 4 per cent of the families
and less than 1 per cent of the
population by individuals - with a "vastly
preponderant majority of the Nation
unaffected" by "speculative gyrations."
From this circumstance, he drew the
conclusion that American purchasing
power ar*4 o' demand for
commodities F Been scarcely touched by
the fall * (jjrurity prices.
Dr. Klein said that it was impossible
for him to forecast what might be
expected on the Stock Exchange
"tomorrow and next week," and Improper, as
well, for a Government official to
attempt to do so.

Psychology Plays Part.
"The careful student of American
economic life," he continued, "equipped
with an abundance of statistics, can
forecast fairly well the long time trend
of production and of standards of
living, and even of many more specific
branchea of business or other
economic aspects. He cannot foresee
accurately short-time changes in
economic conditions and least of all those
speculative changes which depend
largely on the psychology of the people
or of a fraction of the people.
"All of us are justified, in my
opinion, in a profound confidence in the
general economic future of the country.

Just what relation should exist
between that confidence and his present
attitude toward the stock market is
something for each individual to decide
for himself.'*

Sears-1 Roebuck Workers.
Policy of Support Is Same as
Followed in 1921 Period
of Depression.
By the Associated Press.
CHICAGO, October 30 - The Herald
and Examiner said today In a
copyrighted story that Julius Rosenwald,
philanthropist and chairman of the
board of Sears, Roebuck & Co., had
"pledged without limit" his personal
fortune to guarantee the stock market
accounts of the 40,000 employes of his
company.
Mr. Rosenwald decided to take this
action, the paper said, following the
market drop last Thursday. That same
evening he conferred with his son,
Lessing. who is vice president of the
company; Gen. Robert E. Wood, president;
W. O. Lewis, treasurer, and John
Higgins, another vice president. To
Higgins was delegated the duty of seeing
that the employes' accounts were
protected.

Looks Up Accounts.
Higgins immediately looked up the
accounts of all employes, not only in
Chicago, but everywhere the company
has branches. When he found an
employe carrying an account on which, in
the present bear market, his margin
had grown too narrow for safety.
Higgins communicated with the broker
handling the account. •
The broker then was asked whether
additional collateral was needed to
safeguard the account, the Herald and
Examiner said. __
"We simply put up the collateral so
that our employes shall be able to
weather the storm." Higgins explained.

"One of the first things I found out
was that a great many employes will
have no need for the assistance offered.
Some of them, thanks to their thrift
and good judgment, are wealthy. The
help Mr. Rosenwald is offering Is for
those who need it."
Did Same Thing In 1921.
Through Higgins it was learned for
the first time that Mr. Rosenwald
adopted a similar plan during the
period of financial depression in 1921.
"At that time what we did in Mr.
Rosenwald's name was to gather up all
the employe stock acounts that needed
support and place them in the hands
of two big brokerage concerns,
depositing collateral as required. The sum Mr.

Rosenwald then pledged was about sl,-
Also in 1921, It was recalled. Mr.
Rosenwald made a gift of $5,000,000
Worth of his own stock to the company
and Dledged $20,000,000 more of his
personal fortune to see the company
1 present action. It was explained,
applies to all employes' stock accounts,
no matter what stocks the employes
hold.

An aftermath of the

The search for giilty
personalities has become an especially
popular pastime on Capitol
Hil, but has by no means been
limited to political quarters.
The Democratic Senators blame
the Republican administration,
and the Republican solons seek
to fix the responsibility on
Democrats, especially John J.
Raskob, - chairman of tne
Democratic national committee.

These efforts are singularly
childish and naive.
The causes lie deeper in
human nature. At various
interludes in all countries and in
all periods of history, the
public becomes strangely deluded
with a false sense of values.
Intemperateness led to the
building of an inflated price
structure, whose correction was
only a matter of time.
There has been criticism of
the Bix Six bankers, but it is
part "of the record that once
they got started they worked
with rare ingeniuty to turn
back the destructive forces.

The criticism has been made,
however, that they started too
late. One leading independent
financier insists that the
banking consortium, which put in
bids to support pivotal stocks
around mid-day on Black
Thursday, after the beginning
of the collapse, should have had
supporting bids in on previous
days before the great setback
which temporarily destroyed
confidence got under way.
But once the bankers got
organized, they did magnificent
work in mobilizing the
integrating forces of the country.
They doubtless felt that to
place supporting bids too high
would be to invite additional
liquidation. Accordingly, they
placed bids below the market.

Naturally, the shorn lambs are
Irritated at the thought that
the rescuing bankers'
consortium picked up shares at
bargain prices.
They would not expect those
who do relief work at an
earthquake to make handsome
profits. Yet, this fact is per
haps inherent in the nature of
the profits system. The
economic system rewards services,
and it is a service to take
stocks from the market when
the frenzied crowd is seeking
to get rid of them irrespective
of price.
Os course, the difficulties of
the New York bankers - who
labored valiantly to bring
finanlcal order out of chaos.

NO DEPRESSION,

Summing up the general busi
ness and industrial situation in
connection with the stock market
crash. Secretary of Commerce
Lamont said today that "the
country has nothing to worry
about."
Lamont called attention to the
fact that over a long, period
business depressions have been
preceded by factors which are
practically the reverse of underlying
conditions as they exist today.
He believes market losses will to
some degree curtail buying power,
but that this will not prove
serious.
Lamont emphasized particularly
Census Bureau statistics which
showed that in September there
was no increase in inventories as
compared with thi same month
a year ago, and unfilled orders
were greater, while no increase
was noted in commodity prices.

An almost unfailing indicator
of a coming depression- has been
sharp increases in commodity
stocks and an absenceo f unbilled
orders.

In Two Weeks? The Idea!
While President Hoover seemed'
naive in suggesting that the Senate
should pass a tariff bill "within the
'next two weeks,'' he must be
credited with knowing that the wondrous
thing would not happen.
The real point of the suggestion
is in the reminder it carries. It
reminds us that the Senate just now
is the most futile, incompetent
legislative body on the face of the
earth. It has had since last June to
pass a tariff bill, and we are now
on the edge of winter. Senators are
struck with consternation by the
suggestion that they could finally
vote on the bill at the end of two
more .weeks, but that only proves
how inadequate to the situation the
Senate may be. A complete tariff
revision is not called for - only a

partial one. Is there a Parliament
in any other great nation that could
get nowhere in six months on such
a measure, and then insist with
wmunded dignity on at least a
month's more time?
To be sure, the lack of a genuine
and widespread demand for a new
tariff is at the bottom of the
Senate's wrangling impotence. The
Senate's-disintegration reflects popular
indifference. Yet there is something
more, to be said. The constitutional
set-up of the United States
governmenuis capable of utter collapse in
the matter of legislative
responsibilitjcmnder such conditions as have
now arisen. The administration can
exercise no leadership and no
control through majority action. What
a British or French cabinet would
put through in two weeks as part of
the annual budget, or resign, lands
our Congress after six months or
more'in a ditch.

The" President is not now asking
for the passage of the bill in any
special form. He asks merely that
some bill be passed, that a majority
shall function. It cannot be done -
not in two weeks. We don't have
that kind of a government.
[November 2.]

Investigating the Panic
Senator Nye's resolution
providing for a congressional
investigation of the stock market crash is
unlikely "to yield immediate results.
The Senate has several other
investigations already under way. The
exchange of embittered accusations
of political responsibility for the
panic 'reveals the feeling of the
party leaders and for a while they
will be satisfied with blowing each
othef^up while the stock market
crawls out of the cyclone cellar.
E ten t u a 1 Iy, an investigation
should preferably be made, if at all,
by a commission of competent
experts like the national monetary
commission which investigated the
banking situation after the panic of
1907 and prepared the way for the
Federal Reserve act. The panic of
1907 emphasized the serious defects
in the old national banking system.

The country did not have an elastic
currency. A severe "squeeze" in
money could bring on or greatly
intensify a stock market panic, as
was illustrated in 1907.

nonpolitical commission into the

A Changed Situation
The political situation in Congress
has been changed by recent events.
The Republican regulars were
growing thoroughly disgusted and even
reconciled to the tariff bill's
abandonment before the stock market
crashed. Last Saturday evening in
Philadelphia Senator Reed declared
that the tariff bill was dead. Since
then the bottom of the market has
fallen out. In consequence, Senator
Reed's word "dead" fails to describe
the bill's present condition. It may
not be given even a decent burial.

Senator Watson's nervous
breakdown and departure for Florida,
under the orders of his physician,
marks a collapse in the Senate only
less sensational than that in Wall
street. Senator Watson has been
the majority leader since Mr Curtis
became vice-president. He has led
his party into the worst schism it
has experienced since 1909-1911.
The regulars of the majority now
have no leader; a fight is threatened
if they attempt to choose one. Three
days after his Philadelphia speech
Senator Reed is again heard from,
saying: "The bill is dead as a dodo.

'To continue the debate is a
mock'ery. The best thing to do would
'be to adopt a motion of
adjourn'ment. I may offer it myself."
This newspaper said substantially
the same thing last June after the
passage of the farm relief bill. It
claims no credit for superior
discernment, but it so happens that its
apprehensions as to tariff legislation
have been amply confirmed by
events. The regular Republicans are
utterly thwarted in their efforts to
put through a tariff bill in the l ast
to their liking. Senator Moses has
even announced that, if the bill
comes to a vote, he will go on
record against it. For the bill is being
made by the Democrats and the
insurgent Republicans of the West
who, according to the delightful Mr
Grundy, should not be allowed to
participate in tariff legislation at

Within one's memory there has I
been no tariff bill collapse like this
one. President Cleveland in his
second term lost control of his own
party in the Senate. The
Democratic senators followed Mr Gorman
rather than Mr Cleveland, and the
result was the Democratic tariff law
branded by the Democratic
President - who refused to sign it - as
one of "perfidy and dishonor." Yet
the Senate Democrats did get
together sufficiently to put the bill
through. The Senate Republicans of
today have no leader with the power,
resourcefulness and authority of Mr
Gorman of Maryland. They are
split as the Senate Democrats of
1893-1894 never were.

Yet this state of affairs is less
tempting ■to Democrats seeking
partisan advantage than it was a
fortnight or even a week ago. The
Democratic party in the past has
repeatedly suffered loss of prestige
when Democratic tariffs were
followed by stock market panics and
by business depression, or became
identified in the public mind with
fianancial and industrial instability.
t

The Democratic party suffered
heavily for many years because the
Democratic tariff of 1894 was associated
in the public mind with hard times.
One would suppose that the
Democratic leaders would now be

responsibility for, or become in any

legislation sure to be unpopular if the
•uric of the past week should be

major, or even a minor, business

The Democratic party might lose

market crash by seeking to force a

It was really Senator Reed of
Pennsylvania who started the attack
on the cornbelt and cowboy states
in tariff legislation. Mr Grundy, the
head lobbyist of the Pennsylvania
manufacturers, merely echoed Reed.
In his recent Philadelphia speech
Senator Reed put it as follows: -
Of course, the result is that

Thank the Lord, in the House we

the bill in the shape in which it

The senator's cry of gratitude

based on population was in effect
criticism of the Senate in which
each state is entitled only to two
senators. Mr Grundy was merely
more outspoken in saying that states
like Idaho, which pay comparatively
little in taxes into the federal
treasury, should be "silenced" when
legislation of economic importance to

two senators, regardless of
population and wealth, he thought

The Liberia Investigation
A thorough investigation of
charges that slavery, or forced
labor hardly distinguishable from
slavery, exists on a large scale in
Liberia is assured by the broad
scope for the inquiry insisted upon
by the Liberian government, which
feels that it has been slandered.
America will be interested in the
investigation not only because the
United States is to take part, but
because this African free state has
always been of special concern to
us. It is also of interest that the
charge of the revival of slavery has
in some degree been connected with
the provision of labor for the great
Firestone rubber concession.

With so luxuriant a tropical
background scandal flourishes and is
difficult to uproot. So many stories in
regard to Liberia have been in
circulation that an official inquiry is
probably necessary for reassurance,
although their number does not add
to the likelihood of their truth. It
is fortunate that an ideal agency
exists in the League of Nations, and
that the United States, which takes
a special interest in Liberia, should
be able to co-operate.
The chief aim of the inquiry,
indeed, is to determine whether or
not there exists in Liberia slavery
as defined by the League's
antislavery convention which has been
ratified by the United States. The
commission to investigate conditions
will consist of three members, one
each appointed by the United States,
the League of Nations and Liberia.

The participation of the League was
obtained at its recent • assembly by
Liberia, which showed a desire to
have the inquiry made as thorough
as possible.
In its note to the League the
Liberian government asks that the
commission investigate the alleged
existence of slavery, the participation
of the government and of citizens,
and determine to what extent, if
any, forced labor exists and
whether the shipment of contract labor to
Fernando Po or to the Congo is
associated with slavery. In particular
the Liberian government desires to
have the commission determine
"whether the labor employed for
'private purposes on privately owned
'or leased plantations is recruited by
'voluntary enlistments or is forcibly
'impressed by the Liberian
govern'ment or by its authority."
The inquiry is expected to last
four months, and the commission is
authorized by Liberia to summon

witnesses whose attendance will be
made obligatory, and to make such
recommendations to the government
as it sees fit. In this matter
Liberia seems to be acting in good
faith, and it is a pity that some
other countries in which slavery has
been said to flourish have not acted
in the same spirit.
(November I.]

The Guggenhehn Foundation
Although the Daniel Guggenheim
Fund for the Promotion of
Aeronautics is to be dissolved, much of
the work which it has carried on for
the past three years will be
continued through other agencies. It
is announced by Harry F.
Guggenheim, president of the fund, that
the new arrangements include the
establishment of the first
aeronautical engineering school in the South,
the gift to the Library of Congress
of a great collection of books on
aeronautics, the establishment of an
airship institute at Akron, and large
gifts to colleges in the United
States and to aeronautical societies
abroad. These gifts were made
possible by the gift of $500,000 to the
fund by its founder, Daniel
Guggenheim, bringing the total up to $3,-
000,000 in addition to at least a
million which he has devoted in other
ways to the encouragement of
aeronautics.

Discontinuance of the fund as a
separate agency is explained on the
ground that its principal tasks have
been accomplished and that the
growth of interest in aeronautics
gives assurance of progress. From
the first the purpose of the fund
has been to promote safety in the
air, and the two chief difficulties
encountered have been the lack of
stability in plapes and the danger of
flying or alighting in fog. The
solution of the problem of "blind"
flying was announced only a few
weeks ago. By the addition to the
navigation instruments already
available of a few devices worked
out by experts in the service of the
fund it was shown to be possible for
a pilot with the cabin screened so
that he could see only his
instrument board to find the flying field
and to land safely at a designated

spot, his instruments giving him
with precision both his position and
his altitude besides enabling him to
keep his plane on a level keel.
What has been accomplished
toward the solution of the other
principal problems will be shown at a
competition to be held this month
at. Mitchel field, at which a number
of new designs will be tested. The
competition closes November 1, but
novel aircraft are still arriving from
abroad, and the time for their entry
may be stretched a little. The
progress made in the designing of safe
machines in the past three years is
highly encouraging, and not a little
of the credit should go to the Daniel
Guggenheim fund.

The one-sided development of
flying, with undue emphasis upon
speed, has, of course, been due
mainly to military influence. A great
impetus was given to aviation by the
war, but in great part it was an
impetus in the wrong direction. The
average plane was fast enough for
the uses of peace, but very far from
being safe enough. To increase the
popularity of flying it was above
all necessary to produce a useful
flying machine that could take off and
alight at a moderate speed. Many
inventors have been working at this
problem, and several new types have
been reported in which the wings
can be increased in area, making it
possible to land almost at a
standstill.

With the solution of these
fundamental problems in sight the fund is
considered no longer necessary. In
announcing the various gifts for the
continuance of some phases of the
work through other agencies, Harry
F. Guggenheim says: "Private
capital, which is now available in almost
'unlimited amounts for aviation
enterprise, will and properly should
'carry on these fundamental
developments to their commercial
appli'cation." This draws fairly the
dividing line between the province of
an endowment and the province of
enterprise, and the scientific study of
aviation, in so far as a practical use
for it is now in sight, wiH be cared
for by the various institutions to
which gifts have been made. In the
three years of its existence the fund

has pjayed an important part in the
history of aeronautics.

^Financial Strain Eased
Yesterday's stock market not only
saw greatly improved prices
maintained for the second consecutive
day, but the late hours of the
afternoon brought announcements of a
reduction of 1 per cent in the
Federal Reserve rediscount rate and of
a decrease of $1,096,000,000 in
brokers' loans made by and through
member banks at New York. The
compilation of brokers' loans
presumably does not reflect the
substantial advance in the stock
market on Wednesday, but it affords an
impressive index to the liquidation
of the previous week.

The loans total is, indeed, an
index, not a measure. It does not
represent all the borrowings on stock
and bond collateral, and even less
does it represent the rise or
shrinkage in market values. But it has
significance as an index to the credit
situation, and the extraction of sl,-
096,000,000 from stock market
operations in a week made a reduction
of the Federal Reserve rate more or
less automatic. A drop in the
Reserve rate from 6 to 5 per cent at
New York, following a reduction of
the London bank rate yesterday
morning from 6U to 6 per cent,

promises easier money conditions,
and, as there is now less likelihood
of easier money being absorbed by
speculation, the result should be
favorable for business.
Examination of the brokers' loans
statement shows that the New York
banks were called upon to meet a
situation of some difficulty, apart
from any aid which they gave to
the market by the buying of
securities. During the week they
increased their loans on collateral by
over $1,000,000,000, while loans for
the account of "others," who include
corporations, investment trusts and
individuals, dcreased by $1,400,000,-
000. It is assumed that these other
lenders reduced their call money
loans in order to buy securities at
favorable prices. But the sudden
withdrawal of funds which had been
so freely supplied by "others" made
it necessary for the banks to go to
the rescue of the stock market.

Doubtless the. banks experienced
more strain than appeared on the
surface. But they met the situation
quietly and well, and without
increasing the cost of credit
accommodation.
The shrinkage of $1,400,000,000 in
the loans account of nonbanking
lenders has another point of interest
apart from the credit burden
imposed on the banks. Investment trust
funds have been loaned heavily in
the stock market, and it is assumed
that these funds were withdrawn to
be put into investments when it
became possible to buy stocks for a
reasonable yield. But if this was
the case - and it seems altogether
probable - the only conclusion is
that the idle funds of the
investment trusts have been hanging over
the market like a sword of Damocles
for many months. Trusts that were
properly organized and
conservatively managed could not buy
securities while abnormally high price
levels prevailed. It was to their
advantage that the market should go
down. Whether the trusts are going
to be an element of stability or
insecurity in the stock market in the

future is a question for bankers and
the investing community to consider.
There are trusts and trusts.

A Southern Mill Owner's
Testimony
Light from a somewhat unusual
source was shed on the southern
textile mill situation in an address
at New York Wednesday by Henry
P. Kendall of Camden, S. C., at a
"church and textile situation
con'ference" under the auspices of the
social relations department of the
Congregational Education society.
Mr Kendall is connected with the
Kendall mills at Camden and with
mills in other parts of the state.
The general picture that he
presented was similar in outline to the one
that has been made familiar by
"agitators" and social workers.

Mr Kendall explained the origin
and practice of "spreading labor"
that has been the cause of much
of the trouble in southern mills. The
mills in whose management he is
concerned, he said, spent more than
8300,000 in the course of a year and
a half in improving their machinery
with a result that the number of
workers necessary to operate a given
number of spindles was reduced. On
an average an operator who
formerly had tended 27 spindles was able
to tend 117. Rival mills in the
neighborhood, not knowing about
the improvements in machinery but
posted regarding the reduction in
the number of employes per
spindle, attempted to force their
workers to produce the same results with
the old apparatus. In one mill the
new regime lasted just one morning,
when the workers went on strike; in
another the foreman, who had

charge of the "spreading," was
forced to leave town to escape the
wrath of the operatives.
Mr Kendall, agreeing with other
observers, characterizes living
conditions in some of the mill towns as
"really pretty terrible." He had
been told, but did not personally

vouch for it, that in some mill towns
the income of some entire families,
and characteristically large families,
was only about $5 a week.
"Conditions like these, and the
overexpan'sion of the textile industry that has
'been going on in the last nine
'years," he said, "have brought
'things to a point where the
situation only requires a match to set off
'a big explosion."
The prospects for the campaign
which the American Federation of
Labor is entering with much show
of enthusiasm for organization of
the southern mill workers appear
somewhat dubious in the light of
Mr Kendall's characterization of the
typical employe. The mill
operatives, he said, are religious and
fundament«lly conservative; they are
not us-d to living 7a groups anj
they do not take kindly to
organization or group movements. But they
"have no hesitation about taking a

'rifle" ' and when they believe they
are being unjustly dealt with they
are dangerous. "The situation is
'bad enough as it is and the radical
''agitators and organizers are always
'able to capitalize trouble." There
is clearly need of social education
by both employers and employed,
and by the public as well. The
opportunity is great for conservative
unionism to help, but the task that
it has undertaken promises to call
for all of its resources of patience
and diplomacy.

Old Age Pensions in Wisconsin
The supervisors of Milwaukee
county, Wis., accepting the
provisions of a state law amended last
summer, have voted an appropriation
of SIOO,OOO for old age pensions. To
be eligible to a pension a person
must be over 70 years old and must
have been a resident of the county
at least 15 years. The amount of

each pension is limited to $1 a day.
From the discussion of the subject
in the Milwaukee Journal it
appears that granting of pensions,
subject to the limitations named above,
is left in individual cases to the
judgment of the superviso/s. Also
that the state of Wisconsin has
agreed, by the passage of the act,
to contribute to the fund, but that
experience with the results of
similar legislation indicates that it will
fail to provide the funds necessary
to the fulfilment of the agreement.

If the last suggestion is true there
is evidently something the matter
with the state's law-making system.
Illustrating the need of a clear
understanding regarding pension
eligibility, the Journal notes that "it
'is said" that in one county a
supervisor placed his aged mother on the
pension list on the theory that, since
pension money was available, any
aged person might properly collect
it. A common provision in old age
pension laws elsewhere than
Wisconsin is that a person shall be
entitled to a pension only if his total
income from other sources is less
than a specified sum. This seems
fair, although the application of the
principle would not always be easy.

For example, some aged persons
with no definite income are so
provided for in the homes of their
children or elsewhere that their
situation is much more comfortable
than that of others who are virtually
friendless though enjoying a definite
income large enough to disqualify
them as pensioners. On the other
hand, persons in the first group may
enjoy their privileged position at the
expense of others - young children,
for instance - whose claim on the
parental income is not less than the
claim of the aged.

Such questions are not, however,
serious. Experience will aid in
perfecting the pension laws and guiding
their wise administration. The
significant fact is the growing
acceptance of the principle of old age
pensions as economically sound and as
in accordance with the obligations
of the state to those under its
sovereignty. • Not so much is heard as
used to be heard of the idea that old
age pensions would discourage
thrift. Not many persons would
deliberately neglect opportunity to
accumulate riches because of
assurance that otherwise they would get
a dollar a day after 70 - if they
should live that long. On the
contrary, It is reasonable to suppose
that many would continue to work
and accumulate with greater zest if
they were assured that at worst they
could not be reduced to a pauper's
estate in the poorhouse.

A 100-Story Skyscraper
The latest skyscraper
announcement in New York city will
challenge the interest of the general
public, that has become so used to
the constantly growing succession
of record-breaking or near
recordbreaking tall buildings that it has
given up trying to keep track of
them. The new champion, to be
built for the Metropolitan Life
Insurance company on Madison-square,
next to the present Metropolitan
"tower," will have a full 100 stories,
compared with the Woolworth
building's meager 57 stories. The short
history of the skyscraper as the
dominant feature of New York's
architecture may be said to have
begun in 1893, when the Manhattan
Life Insurance building was put up
on lower Broadway. This "tallest
'office structure in the world" was
350 feet high and had 23 stories.

For sometime afterward the Singer
building, a little farther up town,
was the city's architectural wonder.
It is 612 feet, and 47 stories high.
The Metropolitan tower, soon to be
dwarfed by its new sister, or
brother, has 50 stories and rises 700
feet. Already the Wool worth
building has been exceeded in hight - by
the Bank of the Manhattan
building, on Wall street, and the
Chrysler building, on East Forty-second
street.

The architects of the new 100story building are Dan Everett Waid
and Harvey Wiley Corbett, the
latter of whom, as every Springfield
schoolboy and girl should know,
designed our municipal group. The
problem of meeting the conditions
of the city's zoning ordinance and
at the same time assuring utility
and beauty of form has been
interestingly solved. The setbacks are
arranged in rhythmical succession to
carry the eye easily upward while
preserving unity and balance. A
novel feature is the large proportion
of the surface given to the windows,
which are to be of ceiling hight.

The building up to the first setback
is to be surfaced in marble. Above
this the entire building will be
enclosed in metal and glass. The
building will be free from
ornament "which has not a rational
'meaning and practical use."
The building, which Will have
accommodations for 30,000 workers,
will be used exclusively, it is stated,
by the insurance company and its
employes. They will get to the first
13 stories by movable stairways.
Elevators from the ground floor will
give express service te the 13th floc;
and local service from there to the
32d floor. Twenty elevators will
start from that floor, 10 of them
going to the 73d floor and the
others to the 100th. Two basement
floors will be given over to restau-

-rants. Entrance to the present
building and to the Fourth-avenue
subway will also be provided below
ground. It looks as if the subway
were in for crowding when the

Hazard of Great Lakes
The Great lakes, though known
as a region of peril to mariners in
the late fall months, seldom
advertise their danger as cumulatively as
in the past fortnight. On October 22,
the Grand Trunk car ferry Milwau- *
kee left the port for which it was
named at 8 p. m. with 26 loaded
freight cars end a crew of 52
persons on board. Two days later the
bodies of nine members of the crew
were found in lifeboats. No one
lived to tell '/hat happen**/. On
October 29 the steamship Wisconsin
sank near the place where the
Milwaukee is supposed to have gone

down and 12 persons perished, five
times that number being saved by
heroic action of the coast guard and
the crew of a tug. Two days later
two freight steamers were in
collision in a fog off Port Washington,
Wis., and one of them went down
with a death list of seven.
All these disasters occurred in

Lake Michigan. In the well-compiled
government book which serves as a
guide to Great lakes navigation
some threescore wrecks are listed
as a possible menace to merchant
steamers or fishing craft in the
waters of the five lakes. Only two
of this total are in Lake Michigan.
Lake Erie and Lake Superior have
the greatest number of submerged
wrecks, the positions of which are
marked by buoys, although most of
them are not directly in the lanes
of merchant vessels. One might
infer from this list of old wrecks
which have never been removed that
Lake Michigan was the least
dangerous of the Great lakes. The real
reason for this seeming freedom
from disaster is that Michigan is
not one of the lakes of heaviest
traffic. The main routes through the
lakes are from the grain and ore
ports on Superior to the ports of

Lake Erie, which unload the ore and
grain and send back coal. With
three major disasters in 10 days,
Lake Michigan cannot be regarded
as an expanse where handling a
merchant vessel is child's play.
Two of the disasters occurred
during a storm of a severity seldom
matched at this season of the year.
Even the lake front of Chicago,
which is increasingly being
appropriated for civic use and adornment,
became a place of raging wind and
overflowed lake water. Yet each of
the disasters seems to have taken
place because of overconfidence in
the strength of a craft and the skill
of its navigators. On the fatal day
the car ferry had started from
Milwaukee at 2.30 p. m. but had turned
back after encountering the force
of the gale. At 8 p. ml it put out
again, and was at the bottom of the
lake in probably two hours. The
steamer Wisconsin, lost two days

later, was the only large vessel io
make its run the day the car ferry
went down, but that honor was of
small avail.
In each of these cases the cargo
may have shifted and thus imperiled
the ship, but a car ferry with loaded
freight cars or a steamer carrying
iron castings or other heavy freight
must reckon such a possibility
among the normal hazards to be
guarded against. The third Lake
Michigan disaster was simply a
collision in a dense fog - which might
have happened on any body of water
where large vessels ply on regular
courses.

In the case of the car ferry and
the steamer Wisconsin, a sounder
sense of caution would have kept
the vessel in port. Yet each ship
seems to have been in experiened
hands. Where disaster overtakes a
vessel leaving port under a known
hazard, it Is always desirable for
the public to know whether the
captain was free to exercise his own
judgment regarding advisability of
putting but. The wisest captain may
miscalculate. Such errors have to
be accepted as examples of Human
fallibility. But the situation is
different if the mariner responsible for
the operation of the vessel felt
constrained to start because his failure
to do so would involve him in
argument with his general manager or
the owners.

"What do you mean?" asked the
Fox. with a cunning look on his face.

"Just this," explained the Bob Cat.
"As I came past the Police Dog's

his uniform, with its brass buttons,
hanging out on the line. I guess his
wife washed it and put it out to dry.

bed. So you can go down to his back
yard, get his uniform off the line and
bring it here."

' What will you do with it?' aeKeo

"I'll put it on and pretend to be the

"He isn't much bigger than I am.
And when I have on his uniform, And
carry his club, with the sun shining
on the brass buttons and the
nickelplated badge, and with his cap pulled
down over my face - why, I'll look so
much like that Police Dog I'll fool
Uncle Wiggily!"
•'How?" asked the Fox.
"Why," mewed the other, "I'll go
right up to that rabbit's bungalow
and ask him to come out and take a
walk. He'll think I'm the Police Dog
and that it's all right. So he'll come
with me and I'll lead him here and

A little later, wearing the dog's
uniform, the Bob Cat knocked boldly at
Uncle Wiggily's bungalow door.
"Ail, good morning. Police Dog!"
greeted the rabbit politely.
"Good morning!'' said the Bob Cat,
trying to make his voice gruff.
••Wouldn't you like to come for a walk
with me, Uncle Wiggily?"
"Why, of course I would. Police
Dog." said Mr. Longears. "Just a

In the Police Dog's uniform there

Ha! A trick! But you can't fool

went down with the ship.
The Wisconsin, with a heavy cargo

left CTiicago at 7:35 p. m. Monday,
hound for Racine, Milwaukee and
lake points northward. High waves
shifted the cargo and loosened
plates, it is believed. She began
tuking on water rapidly while her
radio operator sent calls for help.

darkness as the old liner slowly
went down, her fires out and her
pumps choked, was told today by

Kenosba hospitals suffering from
exposure and injuries.
"A little after 4 o'clock the
Kenosha coast guard boat arrived,
but the lake was so rough it couldn't
come near us," said Fred Treuber,
Milwaukee, lookout who was taking
orders from Captain Morrison.
"Then the captain ordered the
boats lowered on the port side. The
starboard side was high in the air.

Captain Faces Death
"We never knew wliat a great
man our captain was until this
happened. He was calm, gave his
orders in a clear voice and inspired us
all with his courage. When I got to
the water with the first 15 off I
shouted good-bye to the captain.
" 'Good-bve men,' he answered.* '
John Denier, deck hand, told of
the death of Captain Morrison.
"All the life boats had gone and
the captain ordered the rafts cut
loose. The ship was sinking faster.

We kept begging the captain to
come on.
"After a last look around, he
started toward the life rafts, but it
was too late. The ship gave a lurch.
The prow shot up and then dived
under the water. I thought 1 saw
Captain Morrison swimming. The
next time I saw him he was dead,
being brought in by the coast
guard. ' '
Lake Michigan has claimed at
least 89 lives since Sept. 11 when the
gravel boat Andaste sank with 25
men. The sinking of the Milwaukee
added v'r The Wisconsin's death
list mav reach 12 or more.

I - BINGHAM CONDEMNED
Passage of the Norris resolution condemning Sen*
a tor *nr«w Bingham, of Connecticut, for conduct con*
trary to good morals and Senatorial ethics, tending to
bring the Senate Into dishonor and disrepute, gives
Senator Bingham, as a result of the Eyanson Incident,
the punishment of being the first Senator in modern
times to bring upon himself the formal censure of his
colleagues.
Whll. the punishment Is severe, placing an stigma
on Bingham's whole public career. It Is not too severe
for the offense, which consisted of bringing a
representative of the Manufacturers* Association or
Connecticut Into the Senate and placing him on the
Senate payroll as a tariff "expert".

Bingham says the Incident Is over and he will not
resign. That is his affair. Perhaps he Intends to
remain In the Senate and try to live down one of the
worst mistakes a Senator ever made. But when he
says he will not resign he falls to take Into
consideration tht question of whether his usefulness is over as
a representative of the people of Connecticut. His
mind Is concentrated now on himself, and he Is
thinking of remaining for his own satisfaction. But if
he were a little more sensitive he should see that a
Senator Is somewhat in the same position as a Judge.

The moment a shadow is thrown on his integrity, he
is no longer In a position to discharge fully the duties
for which he was chosen.

THE MEXICAN CODE
The new penal code of Mexico seems to be one of
those things that will enable us to pat ourselves on
the back and reflect on our Immeasurable superiority
to our neighbors south of the Rio Grande.
There Is, for instance, the new law relating to
robbery.
No Mexican, hereafter, can be punished for robbery,
If he can prove that he was hungry at the time he
committed It and that he had never engaged in a
robbery before.
This is Just the sort of thing that will make us feel
that Mexico Is truly a backward nation. There is
something childish, trusting and ingenuous in that
law. Imagine how it would work in a city like - for
instance - Chicago 1 Wouldn't it be a wonderful
defense lor rascals?

Yet, when you stop to think about It, It isn't quite
as laughable as It. sounds.
It may be clumsy and impractical; yet, for all that,
it represents a genuine attempt to put a little
common sense and humanity into the criminal code - and
the criminal code north of the Rio Grande Isn't
exactly bogged down with either of those qualities.
Mexico, clearly, is trying to make her legal
machinery recognize a perfectly obvious fact; that a man can
commit a crime and still not be a real enemy of
society.

Many a robbery' is committed by an ordinarily
lawabiding and upright man who is driven by poverty
and misery to a point where it seems better to commit
a robbery than to starve to death and see his family
starve to death.
In such a case - where it is quite clear that the man
is not a criminal by nature - isn't it better to turn him
loose and give him another chance than to do as we
usually do in the United States - stick him in prison
and Uirn him into a confirmed criminal?

Mexico's new law undoubtedly will help some real
scamps to escape punishment for their misdeeds. But
will that be any worse than some of the savage
injustices that our own laws occasionally cause?

By GEORGE MATTHEW ADAMS.
GENTLENESS
The longer I live, and the more I come In contact
with other human beings, the more I am convinced
that gentleness is one of the rarest and most prized
of all the virtues akin to man.
This human spirit of ours, which is so intricately
housed in a body of wonders, is a most sensitive
gift. Even a child is hurt by a harsh look, though
no words are spoken, proving this delicacy of feeling
which is born in us all.

No matter how strong we may think we are, this
spirit never gets over its sensitiveness. Deeply
hidden is Its eternal longing for gentleness and
consideration.
All great men and women have been gentle in their
attitud toward others, even though at times they
have been the moving spirits in world events. What
a gentle man was Lincbln! And Premier Ramsay
MacDonald, what a man of gentleness and beauty of
character he 1s.
The other day I stood beside the great
co-discoverer of radium, Mme. Marie Curie. I felt as though
a breath of Heaven had passed through me as I
viewed that simple gentlewoman, who went through
such great privation even sacrificing much of her
very body, that she might render service to all
humanity Her silvered hair, the beautiful lines of her
face, those hands that had given of their very flesh

to science - oh. what a woman she was!
What we know of Jesus is that He stands out as
the most gentle of men. Even Pontius Pilate was
so mpressed with Him that he shrank from His
piercing glance, desiring to wash his hands of all ,
guilt in condemning Him. If the religion of
Christianity means anything at all. it means gentleness.
When wa^ay that a man is a gentleman, we mean
that he is sincerely a gentle man.
The longest life is so short anyway in which to
render service, so that to be gentle and to be kind
is no small, or unimportant task! J

'DOUBLY EMPHATIC"
The following letter has been
received from Percy Lambert Hopkins
of Brooklyn, N. Y.:
"I have been reading your column
for many years, and I have always
found it a source of enjoyment and
help. I can frankly say that I have
learned much about our mother
tongue through the instructions I
have received from 'The Right Word,'
and that I wouldn't be without it for
anything.
''Recently I have had a discussion
about what I believe you call the
double comparative. The special
sentence that caused the discussion was
as follows: 'It Is considerably more
warmer today than it was yesterday.

''A friend of mine made this
statement at a time when I could not
comment upon it, as there were others
present. However, later I called the
error to his attention, and he
defended the phrase 'more warmer,' and
said that it made his idea doubly
emphatic.
"I laughed at him and told him he
was just stubborn, but he stood his
ground. Finally I told him I would
write you and let him see for himself
how wrong he was. Therefore, will
you be so kind as to comment on this
error in your column. It will not only
help me to convince my friend of his
mistake, but it will also no doubt help
others to avoid the mistake. I thank
you in advance for your promptness
in discussing this problem."
Answer: Mr. Hopkins, tell your
friend that a double comparative is

wrong, even if used for emphasis.
One may say ''more warm" or
"warmer," but never "more warmer."
Maybe your friend was teasing you.
It does not seem possible that ne
would insist on using a double
comparative.

The Creative Spirit vs. Self-Expression.
How the youngsters will talk about self-expression! And the worst of It
is it is not always limited to talk. A boy gets the idea into his head that this
is the age where youth expresses itself, so he pounces upon his dad's
automobile and races to the nearest roadhouse. A girl thinks she has made the

grandest discovery oi tne age wnen sue imagines tnat sne
can never amount to anything unlesa she stays out until
2 a. m. against her parents wishes and "expresses herself.''
Self-Expression is really the expression of one's self.
Therefore if there is nothing more to a young girl than
a desire to stay out until the wee small hours against her
parents wishes, we have a rather good measure of that
girl's self. But what a mean little self that is. What a
no-account self!

And what shall we say of the boy whose self is so pesky
small that all he can think of to do with his self in
order that it may be expressed is to race up and dowTn
f

that be true, then what a mighty petty self he has!
If he had only said: "I am deliberately doing what other people do not
want me to do for the sake of hurting them," that would be another matter.
We'd call it obstinacy or meanness or cussedness or what have you.
Now, my young friends, honest-to-goodness self-expression involves the
creative spirit. It is positive and not negative. Instead of talking about
what it will not do it gees ahead and does something positive and useful.

Right Kind of Self-Expression
True self-expression finds outlets in literature, music, art, handiwork of
all kinds, in formulating ideas and expressing them, in leading a cause, in
acting contrary to the established order for the sake of a principle.
You know me well enough to know that I do not think the world is going
to the bow-wows; but if I were looking for a reason for thinking so I should
lay it to one tiring; The absence, in the general run of our young people, of
creative work. There's nothing creative in listening to a radio, driving an
automobile, yelling one's head off at a game, shaking one's feet at the
average dance, wearing what everybody else wears and doing what everybody
else does.

For years the Youth's Companion had a department which was a great
force in re-establishing the creative spirit in youth - a spirit which really
never dies when it is once fed. The St. Nicholas League, sponsored by the
magazine of similar name, conducts a competition each month in poetry,
drawing, puzzles, photographs and short story writing. This is a fine way
of encouraging boys and girls in honest to goodness self-expression, J.
Deems Taylor, a composer of a very successful American Opera, when a boy
was a member of this league. So also were Edna St. Vincent Millay, Stephen
V. Benet, William Benet and Lyle Saxon. The Junior Achievement League,
with headquarters In Springfield, Mass., does splendid work In fostering the
creative spirit of youth. And last, but not least, the 4 H club.

Break your neck, boys, if you must, flying a home-made airplane and
charge it up to "self-expression" of the right sort. Break it by speeding
head-on against a tree and put it under the column "damphoollsms." Wear,
girls, if you will, a color which becomes you and itemise it under "creative
spirit." Do something which everybody does and which you shouldn't do and
label yourself "Weak Sister."
Possess a good self and then express that self all you can.

24 [Thursday.] Two Negroes living in Jeffersonville, Ind., were arrested late last night after a large sedan had been removed from' the railroad tracks just before President Hoover's train passed. The sedan was discovered on the tracks five miles north of New Albany, Ind., which is across the river from here. It was removed by residents of the neighborhood a few minutes before the President's train reached the point. The Negroes, Young Wright, 43, and Charies Burlock, 19, were reported to have confessed to detectives that they placed the sedan on the tracks in a plot to obtain money from the railroad company for damages.
